No new permission action: evaluation/handoff reuse `OPS:Edit`, override/revoke-override reuse the already-registered `OPS:Override` (already exercised by `OPS-168`'s own `app.override_job_order_field`), matching `OPS-178`'s own "reuse an existing action" precedent. Evidence checked per non-cancelled Shipment Order belonging to the Job Order: delivery+ePOD completion (`status in ('epod', 'closed')`, the only two statuses reachable via `OPS-177`'s own completion function), the document checklist (`OPS-176`'s own missing-mandatory-items query inlined), no active operational exception (`OPS-174`'s own `status not in ('resolved', 'closed')`), and an approved actual cost (`OPS-178`'s own `is_current and status = 'approved'`). The customer billing-profile check reuses `app.job_orders.credit_snapshot` verbatim -- the exact `{outcome, checkedAt}` object `COM-164`'s own `app.prepare_job_order_handoff` already pinned from the account's most recent credit check at handoff time, the same "read the governed snapshot verbatim" discipline `OPS-179` established for `revenue_snapshot`; `outcome = 'allow'` is ready, a null snapshot (`billing_profile_missing`) or any `blocked_*` outcome (`billing_profile_not_cleared`) is not. `rule_version` is a fixed, disclosed placeholder (`1`) -- no configurable rule-engine table exists yet, the same class of disclosed simplification as `OPS-179`'s "no FX conversion" boundary. Versioned, `is_current`-exclusive; the first evaluation needs no reason, every subsequent evaluation while a current row exists requires a non-empty `reevaluation_reason`, and always resets any prior override (evidence changes do not silently preserve readiness). Override is bounded to forcing an evaluated `not_ready` row to an effective `ready` outcome, never the reverse -- `effective_status` is a **generated column** (`ready` while `is_overridden`, else the evidence-based `evaluated_status`), so the raw evidence result stays visible even while overridden; revoking restores it without ever re-evaluating evidence itself. A minimal, fast, read-only public tracking surface: an unguessable per-shipment opaque token (`COM-154`'s own `token_hash = encode(digest(raw_token, 'sha256'), 'hex')` pattern, raw token returned exactly once at issuance, never stored) resolves to a sanitized status/timeline/ePOD-availability projection -- never a live Customer Portal. `app.lookup_public_shipment_tracking` is the one function in this schema granted `EXECUTE` to `anon` directly (a disclosed, deliberate exception to the standing `ERR-2026-004` revoke-then-explicit-re-grant convention) -- authorization is the token itself, not `auth.uid()`. It is designed to **never raise for an expected outcome** (`not_found`/`invalid`/`rate_limited`): it always returns exactly one row with a `lookup_status` column, every other column null unless `lookup_status='ok'`. This is a direct application of the defect class `OPS-175` first documented for its own dispatch failure-audit design -- a raised exception aborts the whole enclosing transaction (one PostgREST call is exactly one transaction), rolling back any insert made earlier in that same transaction, so a "log the failed attempt, then raise" pattern would silently never persist `app.tracking_lookup_attempts`. Rate limiting counts `not_found`/`invalid` attempts for a caller-supplied `client_key` (a sha256 hash of the caller's own best-effort IP, computed by the calling page/Server Action, never a raw IP stored server-side) in the trailing 15 minutes; 10 or more flips the outcome to `rate_limited`. The sanitized milestone timeline reuses `OPS-173`'s own `is_customer_visible` flag; `epod_available` is a boolean derived from `OPS-177`'s completed ePOD captures -- never the evidence itself. (2) a race between overlapping TCP `'data'` events on the same connection (an un-awaited async call mutating closure-captured state) -- self-diagnosed by reasoning through Node's own event-loop semantics before writing the integration test, fixed by serializing per-connection chunk processing through a promise chain with a terminal `.catch()` guard; Two genuinely concurrent, individually legitimate reparent calls whose locked row pairs are fully disjoint (e.g. `reparent(A, new_parent=D)` and `reparent(C, new_parent=B)`, neither call ever reading a row the other has locked) could each pass their own cycle check against pre-race state and both commit -- together forming a real, permanently-persisted cycle in the package hierarchy, directly violating Prompt 237 §24 ("package identity and hierarchy are stable and cannot cycle") and §33's own acceptance criterion. Both reviewers independently live-reproduced this against a real, freshly-migrated Postgres database using two genuinely concurrent psql sessions with disjoint pre-locking, confirming a real, persisted 4-node cycle (`A->D->C->B->A`) with both RPC calls returning success -- no error, silent corruption, and no table-level CHECK or trigger catches a cycle deeper than immediate self-parent. Fixed by locking every node visited during the ancestor walk (`for update` added to the walk's own `SELECT`), not just the two endpoints -- any two concurrent reparents that would together form a cycle now necessarily contend on a real row lock somewhere in the two walks, and Postgres's own deadlock detector correctly aborts one of them (a normal, retryable `deadlock detected` error), while the survivor's walk always observes fully-committed state. Re-verified live with the identical two-session repro against the patched function: the first session committed normally, the second failed cleanly with a genuine deadlock error and rolled back with no partial writes -- final state a clean tree, no cycle. Two damage shapes: silent misattribution (wrong row returned) and silent no-op (the requested operation skipped entirely while appearing to succeed -- a scanned package line never recorded, a pick never confirmed, a shipment never load-confirmed; real warehouse work never reaching the ledger). Root cause: `drainAccumulator` snapshotted the accumulator and wrote it back via a `commit` callback that destroyed bytes appended during the await. Fixed by sharing one `ConnectionBuffers` holder by reference and consuming each decoded prefix **before** the following await. **F-3 (High)**: `DurableTelemetryBuffer.flush()` rewrote the whole queue file from a stale snapshot, destroying any batch `enqueue()` appended during the flush -- the durable buffer losing precisely the telemetry it exists to protect. go through the two owner-scoped, permission-gated RPCs), matching this same migration's own precedent for `app.notification_delivery_attempts`/`app.workflow_transition_history`. **HIGH `created_at` column with strict inequality, silently and permanently dropping every row sharing an exact timestamp tie at a page boundary — live-reproduced as total data loss (5 tied rows, page 2 returned 0) — fixed with a composite `(created_at, id)` keyset cursor (`DROP`+`CREATE`+re-`GRANT`, a genuine signature widening), with a deliberately-reasoned minimum-uuid fallback for a legacy single-timestamp caller (a maximum-uuid fallback was considered and rejected because it would repeat the boundary row forever at page size 1). **HIGH (correctness/concurrency)** — the vendor-risk and Scan` after, contradicting the migration's own "already covers this migration's own WHERE/GROUP BY shapes" design-note claim — fixed by adding the tenant predicate to both LATERAL joins (swept ## 6. Ledger maintenance rules

1. Update the active index and detailed record in the same checkpoint.
2. Never delete failed/rolled-back records; preserve recovery evidence.
3. Link decisions, errors, issues, changes, and build logs by stable IDs.
4. Do not mark `READY` from optimism; entry dependencies must be evidenced.
5. Reconcile status with `CARGOGRID_BUILD_STATUS.md` after every transition.
6. A task without documentation and last-known-good checkpoint cannot be `COMPLETED`.
